Fixed or Variable, on Both Sides

Most people fix the mortgage and leave everything else on a variable rate. Looked at closely, that's often exactly the wrong way round.

If you're like most households, you've fixed the mortgage and left everything else floating. It's worth asking whether that was a decision or just what happened, because on the numbers it's often the wrong way round.

What fixing actually buys

Fixing doesn't buy you a lower rate. On average, over time, it costs slightly more, because the lender's pricing in the risk they're taking off your hands.

What it buys you is certainty, and certainty is worth most where a rate change would hurt most. So the useful question isn't "will rates rise?" — nobody knows — it's "which of my debts would a rate rise hurt most, and have I protected that one?"

Ranking your debts by rate sensitivity

Two things decide how much a rate rise costs you on a given debt: the balance and the remaining term. Large and long means maximum exposure; small and short means almost none.

Which usually gives you this order:

  1. The mortgage. Largest balance, longest term. A one-point rise here costs more in pounds than a one-point rise on everything else put together. That's why fixing the mortgage is conventional wisdom, and the conventional wisdom is right.
  2. Any second charge or homeowner loan. Same logic, smaller balance.
  3. Credit cards and overdrafts. Variable by nature and repriceable at will. Usually smaller balances, but the rates start high, and card rates move for reasons that have nothing to do with the Bank of England.
  4. Personal loans and car finance. Almost always fixed at the outset in the UK, so there's frequently nothing to decide. Worth checking rather than assuming.

The check most people skip. Rather than reasoning about it, model it. Put every variable-rate balance through the rate stress test and the mortgage through the payment change forecaster, at the same rate rise. Add up the extra monthly cost. That total is your genuine exposure, and it's usually larger than expected, because nobody had totalled it before.

Choosing a fixed period

Longer fixes cost a little more and protect you for longer. The trade isn't really about rates, though. It's about your life:

  • Go short if you might move, if your income's about to change materially, or if you expect to make large overpayments that a longer deal's terms would restrict.
  • Go long if you're staying put, your budget's tight enough that a payment rise would genuinely hurt, and you'd rather not think about it.
  • Either way, watch the early repayment charge. A five-year fix you exit in year two can cost thousands. The ERC schedule is the part of the deal worth reading properly — it's where a long fix stops being free optionality and becomes a commitment.

One thing worth checking that people often miss: whether the deal is portable. A portable mortgage can move with you to a new property, which keeps a good rate through a move and avoids the ERC. It isn't automatic, and it isn't guaranteed at the time you move — you still have to qualify on the new property — but knowing where you stand is worth doing before you sign a five-year deal.

Trackers, discounts and the standard variable rate

Three different things get called "variable", and they behave differently:

  • A tracker follows the Bank of England base rate by a set margin. It moves when base rate moves, transparently and by a known amount.
  • A discount is a reduction from the lender's own standard variable rate. Since the lender sets that rate themselves, they can move yours without base rate moving at all.
  • The standard variable rate is the lender's default, where you land when a deal ends. It's typically well above what you could arrange elsewhere, and drifting onto it is one of the most common avoidable mortgage costs there is.

If you want variable, a tracker is the honest version: you can see what governs it. A discount off an SVR hands the lender a discretion you can't control.

The answer for most people

Fix the mortgage, for a period matched to how settled your life is. Then, instead of leaving the rest floating by default, look at your variable-rate balances and clear them rather than trying to protect them — because on unsecured debt the interest rate is high whether it's fixed or variable, and removing the balance is worth far more than fixing the rate on it. The overpayment calculator will show you what that's worth, and it's usually a better return than any mortgage decision available to you.
